speakers.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
speakers.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I thank the Minister for the Statement and Sir David Bell, his team and those who gave evidence, often at real personal cost. We on these Benches welcome the review and the Government’s acceptance of all 27 recommendations. Every school day, British children are abused for being Jewish, in the one place their parents should be able to trust that they are safe. We heard the headlines yesterday: nearly three in five Jewish students have experienced antisemitism and half of Jewish teachers experienced it at work in the past year—racism in their classroom and workplace. It is intolerable. There is worse in the report’s annex; 16% of this racism is inflicted by teachers, and 38% of the antisemitism students witnessed took place during lessons. Only 18% say an antisemitic incident is actually recorded as such. Two-thirds of Jewish respondents said that antisemitism is not even treated as racism in their school. Yesterday, the Secretary of State told the other place that teachers hear “age-old tropes in the classroom” and do not tackle them “for fear of reprisals”. She said: “The fears about not being politically impartial are hampering our teachers and school leaders, preventin
contributions.name: Baroness Cash

contributions.text: My Lords, the findings of this review are deeply disturbing, with one in five students who responded to the survey reporting that they had witnessed antisemitism and three in five Jewish students saying they had experienced it. Behind these stats are young people who should be concentrating on their education, building friendships and planning their futures, but instead they face prejudice, intimidation and fear because of their religious identity. I say this as a member of a religious minority. I know at first hand from these experiences, whether as a parent or as a youth worker, what can happen to young people when they are discriminated against because of who they are and events over which neither they nor their parents have any control. No child should feel compelled to hide their faith to feel safe at school or college, and also on the journey to school and college. I was horrified to see a video of a parent with a young child from a Jewish community who was being harangued on the Tube. Ironically, it was a Muslim woman in a hijab who challenged it. I do not know how old that video was, but it was quite disturbing that our young people are also fearing facing that intimidation
contributions.name: Lord Mohammed of Tinsley

contributions.who: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions (Baroness Smith of Malvern) (Lab)
contributions.text: My Lords, as both noble Lords have strongly identified, antisemitism is a scourge that has no place in modern Britain and in our schools and colleges. Yet Sir David Bell’s independent review makes it clear that it is a growing and increasingly normalised form of hatred, with too many Jewish pupils, students and staff experiencing its effects in schools and colleges. The findings are a stark reminder that we cannot be complacent. That is why the Government welcome Sir David Bell’s report, thank those who took part—in some cases at considerable risk and detriment to themselves, as the noble Baroness said—and accept all 27 of its recommendations. The review provides a clear and practical blueprint for action. It recognises, as noble Lords have said, that every school, college and teacher has a responsibility to identify, challenge and prevent antisemitism wherever it occurs, ensuring that all young people can learn in an environment that is safe, respectful and free from discrimination. Our focus must now be on implementation. Accepting the recommendations is only the beginning. Delivering meaningful and lasting change will require sustained effort across the sector. To support this w
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, as the former chairman of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, I welcome the report with some degree of enthusiasm. Sir David has produced a very thoughtful report. Does the Minister agree that, vital though it is to adopt the IHRA working definition, the greater challenge is to ensure that it is properly understood and implemented? In particular, the definition is intended as an educational tool to assist in recognising and reflecting on antisemitism, rather than as an instrument to denounce or silence others. That is its strength; it is designed to make people think. The opponents of the definition are those who prefer slogans to thought. Will she ensure that the implementation of the definition this year will be very carefully monitored?
contributions.name: Lord Pickles

contributions.text: I completely agree with the noble Lord. He is right. If anywhere should be enabling careful consideration and education it is our schools and colleges. That is why we are clear that they should not only adopt the definition but, in the way he has described, use it to support teaching and deeper understanding among their pupils.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, the report by Sir David Bell has finally brought to national attention the defects in Holocaust education as it exists today. The report says that antisemitism should be at the heart of it, yet this Government shamefully rejected an amendment from the noble Lord, Lord Verdirame, and me earlier this year that would have confined the proposed learning centre in Westminster to antisemitism. In other words, the Government sought to water it down. That should be changed. We need to review Holocaust education. As the report said, we need teaching about Judaism, contemporary antisemitism and contemporary Jewish life. The little cramped underground learning centre proposed for Victoria Tower Gardens does not tackle that at all; it is about some niche interest relating to the British reaction to the Holocaust. We need fresh thinking. The funds are there. The Government must lead the way and make sure that children are taught about today’s Jews and not, as the report said, that everything ended at the end of the Second World War.
contributions.name: Baroness Deech

contributions.text: There is nothing niche about the responsibility for our schools to teach about the Holocaust. That is within the current national curriculum and will be retained in the future national curriculum. We are clear that education about Jewish life and Jewish people should not start and end with the Holocaust. Sir David made a very important point about how we need to do more to educate our children about Jewish lives, culture and contributions in this country and internationally. That will be a key part of the work we take forward.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, we quite rightly never accuse Muslims or give them responsibility when an Islamic state hangs gay people from a crane in Iran or denies women their rights in Afghanistan, yet there seems to be something about a Jewish state doing something that people do not like that enables them to take it out on Jews altogether. This report will need our teachers to do the work, and we are already hearing that some of them are denying this report. Therefore, my question to my noble friend is: will she ensure that every teacher is given proper antisemitism training, because otherwise this will never happen? If they do not understand the pogroms of the 19th century or the events before the Second World War or actually going back even further, how are they going to be able to make sure that our children are also taught properly?
contributions.name: Baroness Hayter of Kentish Town

contributions.text: Just to be clear, I do not think it is fair to say that the vast majority of teachers are denying this report; nor are, in fact, the vast majority of trade unions or their members. It is important to be clear about that. My noble friend is right to say that this will need support for teachers. That is why this Government have already, as part of the £7 million invested in tackling antisemitism, provided support, sponsorship, champions and resources that will enable teachers more effectively to tackle antisemitism and teach the full range of issues that I touched on in my previous answer. It is why the revision of teacher standards and the focus in teacher training is also something that we will take forward as part of the approach to implementing Sir David’s recommendations.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, Judaism is a religion, but Jewishness is a racial identity, as has long been recognised in UK law. As this report says, antisemitism needs to be treated like any other form of racism. Recently, however—within the last month, I think—the hate crime statistics were published, in which, if memory serves, antisemitic abuse was classified only as religious hate. Will the Minister ask the Home Office to go back and look at this, because to classify it only as a religious hate crime is not sufficient? Perhaps antisemitism needs to have its own category in the hate crime statistics, but in any case the racial dimension of antisemitism needs to be recognised alongside any religious dimension.
contributions.name: Baroness Ludford

contributions.text: My Lords, I think the noble Baroness’s point is right, which is one of the reasons why my right honourable friend the Secretary of State will also be working with the Office for Equality and Opportunity to ensure that the issues identified in this report are taken forward across government.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, we have seen the unintended consequences of removing direct curriculum scrutiny by Ofsted in 2005, and it is under the current Government that the partial reinstatement made in 2019 was once again removed. Can the Minister commit to reversing these decisions, which have made it too easy for politicisation and failures of impartiality in curriculum and teaching to go undetected, thus creating the environment in which antisemitism can flourish?
contributions.name: Baroness Spielman

contributions.text: I am not sure that I quite agree with the noble Baroness about the chain of causation that she suggests in that question, but I have already been clear about the way in which we expect there to be accountability of teachers and representation of the issues in this report in standards. I have also outlined the work that we will do with Ofsted on this.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I very much welcome Sir David Bell’s report, and I congratulate him on his recommendations. I am also delighted that the Government have decided to support them all. There are just two points I would like to raise with the Minister. The first is that we must remember that this report is not just about schools; it is about colleges as well. It is interesting that the noble Baroness, Lady Cash, speaking for the Opposition, did not say a single word about colleges; she only talked about schools and teachers, and she did not mention lecturers either. I hope, therefore, that the Minister will ensure that they do not get forgotten. My second point is that Sir David Bell quite rightly said that we should not just be teaching about the Holocaust. We must get a better understanding among children and young people of the enormous contribution that the Jewish population has made, not just to the economy but to science, literature, the arts and the creative industries as well. Will she ensure that the implementation group particularly looks at this issue and determines how we are going to get the curriculum to adequately reflect the great contribution the Jewish community has made, b
contributions.name: Baroness Blackstone

contributions.text: Yes, my noble friend is absolutely right. We need to tackle antisemitism not only by confronting hatred when it occurs, but also by helping more young people in our schools and—she is right—in our colleges to encounter and understand Jewish life, culture and history, building understanding and challenging prejudice before it takes hold. That will be an important part of this work.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, every one of Sir David Bell’s 27 recommendations is framed as “should” and not “must”—a Civil Service device I remember well from my own time in government. Schools, like civil servants, treat “should” as advisory rather than compulsory. Without firm requirements, practice will vary from school to school; so which recommendations will the Government place on a statutory footing, and will antisemitism training for staff be mandatory?
contributions.name: Baroness Finn

contributions.text: The noble Baroness may have tried to get out of her responsibilities in that way when she was in government, but this Government will not. We have been very clear about the spirit and the word of accepting the recommendations in this report. That is why we are setting up the implementation group, and we will expect Sir David Bell to report on how well the recommendations are being implemented in a year.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I declare an interest as the former chair of the Equality and Human Rights Commission in the past year. It is, of course, the Equality and Human Rights Commission upon which it falls to investigate antisemitism in political parties, which is taking root and is reflected in society and in educational institutions, as we have heard. I am concerned that the Government’s newly framed Islamophobia definition seems to be treated within government—and therefore permeating through to civil society groups—as equivalent to the definition of antisemitism, which, of course, as we have heard this morning, is defined in statute as part of race as well as religion. In the hierarchy of a non-statutory policy, which they say anti-Muslim hostility is, versus antisemitism, there is no comparison of the gravity. Antisemitism in relation to discrimination has to be the policy which the Government take forward at speed and with alacrity. Will she please speak to her colleagues to say that there is no parity of esteem between a policy adopted by government and the law of the land as it stands today?
contributions.name: Baroness Falkner of Margravine

contributions.text: I hope that the noble Baroness can see that the seriousness with which the Government have taken the issue of antisemitism, the Government’s response to Sir David’s recommendations and the work that will follow will show the priority that this Government are giving to tackling antisemitism, given its prevalence and, sadly, its growth in recent years. We are absolutely clear on the priority that we are giving to this work.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I thank the Secretary of State for stating clearly that targeting British Jews and blaming them for events in the Middle East or for actions of the Israeli Government is antisemitism. Can the Minister, then, commit to setting out this principle explicitly in the strengthened political impartiality guidance? I welcome the acceptance of Sir David Bell’s timely recommendations, but following the question of the noble Baroness, Lady Finn, what consequences will there be for breaking these guidelines or for continuing antisemitic behaviour in schools?
contributions.name: Baroness Altmann

contributions.text: The question about accountability is very fair. That is why I took some time in my first response to spell out the placing of these issues, both within teacher standards and teacher training, and in the work of Ofsted and the Independent Schools Inspectorate on the thematic work that I identified. Of course, the Government will take accountability in asking Sir David Bell to report back after a year on the progress that is made on these recommendations as well.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I welcome this review and its very important 27 recommendations. It shines a spotlight on the horrors facing Jewish students, teachers and parents across our country in schools and colleges—horrors that I know all too well as the parent of two primary-aged children attending a Jewish school. To focus on modern manifestations of antisemitism, we know that antisemitism remains, in some instances, under the cloak of anti-Zionist rhetoric. We have only to look at the motion that was passed recently at the Green Party conference to see just one example of such antisemitism. Can my noble friend the Minister say what plans the Government have to ensure that this specific form of antisemitism, which I name anti-Zionist rhetoric, is appropriately captured and understood in all our classrooms?
contributions.name: Baroness Berger

contributions.text: That may well be an important element to reflect in the new curriculum in thinking about the way schools address this issue. I will not comment on the Green Party, although my noble friend is right about the very backward step that motion represents for that party and the sad impact that it will have on those people who most need our protection, not that type of political activity.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I want to come back to the point raised by my noble friend Lady Cash on the NEU, and I welcome the comments from the Minister about her own opinion of its rejection of the IHRA definition. What does she think Jewish families, children and teachers will feel if that union is still allowed to attend meetings specifically on this topic?
contributions.name: Baroness Barran

contributions.text: The Secretary of State and I have been very clear about our position as Ministers and the support we will provide to those families. It is for the NEU to answer that question; I have made my views clear.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I cannot speak for teachers as a whole but, as a teacher, I wonder whether the Minister agrees that the crucial part of the review was the sentence: “I do not believe that encouraging empathy or asking people to consider how others might feel amounts to a restriction on free speech; rather, it is an important part of living and learning together in a diverse society”. Sir David also talks a lot about updating Keeping Children Safe in Education. I once again implore the DfE to publish that in the summer term so that safeguarding leads can absorb it before the autumn.
contributions.name: Lord Hampton

contributions.text: The noble Lord identifies an important part of the report. I agree with his focus on that and with what I think was his view that the vast majority of teachers would also think that that was important. I also hear him on the key point about Keeping Children Safe in Education; an important point in the report was that tackling antisemitism should be seen as a core element of safeguarding, which is why it should be included as a specific issue within the Keeping Children Safe in Education guidance.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I start by registering my disappointment that there are no representatives of the Green Party here to hear this debate. That is a sadness and disappointing. I very much welcome this report, which is both chilling and timely. Also, more importantly, the Government’s response is overwhelmingly positive. We can all applaud them for that. I have one small concern, which is that the Government do not intend to measure the uptake of the IHRA definition until the 2027-28 survey, which leaves well over a year before there is any real scrutiny. Do the Government have any plans to monitor this in the meantime until that takes place? In the meantime, will there be some training for teachers to help them deal with real-life incidents in their classrooms while we await the measurement system?
contributions.name: Lord Grade of Yarmouth

contributions.text: Yes. Not only have we already started some of the training that the noble Lord asks about with the additional investment that we have put into tackling antisemitism in education, but it is an important element of the recommendations that we produce much clearer guidance and resources for teachers. We aim to do that as quickly as possible.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, does my noble friend agree that, rather than risk slipping into a blame game in response to the report, what our schools and colleges may benefit from most is practical support to help them confidently identify what contemporary antisemitism looks like and the consequences for us all of failing to tackle it?
contributions.name: Lord McCabe

contributions.text: My noble friend is absolutely right. That is why I have emphasised—my right honourable friend the Secretary of State emphasised this yesterday and has been very clear in her leadership on it—that it is not enough to condemn what we see in our schools, which quite rightly has happened across the Chamber, notwithstanding some absences; it is also important to provide practical support for teachers in the classroom and for school leaders at times when they face difficult issues that they want to be able to respond to confidently. That is all part of the Government’s plan to respond to this report.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions
